title: Deep learning from scratch
source_deliverable: Digit classification with MNIST. Build a neural network to classify handwritten digits (0 to 9).
summary: Build a neural network from the neuron upwards: what a layer does, why activation functions are needed, how backpropagation adjusts the weights in plain words, how to train and validate a network, and how the same model looks in Keras.
outcomes: Describe what a neuron computes and what a layer of neurons does.
Explain why an activation function is needed between layers.
Describe backpropagation as measuring how much each weight contributed to the error and nudging it in that direction.
Train a network, read a learning curve, and tell overfitting from learning.
Build, train and evaluate a digit classifier with Keras or an equivalent library.

lessons.title: From one neuron to a network
lessons.goal: Explain what a single artificial neuron computes and how stacking neurons into layers builds a model.

sections.heading: One neuron, one number
sections.intent: Describe a neuron as a weighted sum plus an offset, connecting directly to the dot product and gradient lessons.

sections.heading: Layers pass numbers to layers
sections.intent: Explain that a layer takes a row of numbers and produces a new row of numbers, and that the width of each layer is a choice you make.

sections.heading: Where the numbers come from
sections.intent: Explain that the weights start as random values and are the only thing training changes.

sections.heading: Why bother with layers
sections.intent: Give a plain comparison: a linear model draws one straight boundary, a network can draw a curved one, at the cost of more numbers to get right.

lessons.task: For a neuron with weights [0.5, -2, 1] and bias 1, compute the output for the input [3, 1, 4] before any activation function. Then say what the bias does.
quiz: What does a single neuron compute before its activation function?
What can a multi-layer network draw that a single linear model cannot?

lessons.title: Activation functions
lessons.goal: Explain what an activation function does and choose between sigmoid, tanh and ReLU for a hidden layer.

sections.heading: Why a layer needs an activation
sections.intent: Show that without an activation function, stacking linear layers still gives one linear result, so the network gains nothing.

sections.heading: Sigmoid and tanh
sections.intent: Describe both as smooth ways to squash a number into a range, and note that they saturate and slow learning when their input is far from the middle.

sections.heading: ReLU
sections.intent: Explain ReLU as 'keep what is positive, zero the rest', why it is fast, and when it can get stuck.

sections.heading: Choosing the output activation
sections.intent: Explain that a binary task uses one sigmoid output, a multi-class task uses one output per class with softmax, and a regression task uses no activation at all.

lessons.task: Compute the sigmoid of 0 and of 2 to two decimal places, describe in one sentence what ReLU does to a negative number, and say which output activation you would use for the ten digit classes.
quiz: What happens if you stack layers without any activation function?
What does ReLU do to a negative input?
Why does a ten class problem need ten outputs instead of one?

lessons.title: How a network learns: backpropagation in plain words
lessons.goal: Describe backpropagation as a two-step loop of measuring each weight's contribution to the error and adjusting it, without needing the calculus behind it.

sections.heading: The loss measures how wrong you are
sections.intent: Introduce mean squared error and cross-entropy loss as the number the training loop tries to push down.

sections.heading: Step one: blame the weights
sections.intent: Explain the backward pass as working backwards from the error to work out how much each weight contributed, using the gradient idea from the maths module.

sections.heading: Step two: nudge the weights
sections.intent: Explain the update as subtracting a small part of the gradient, and what the learning rate controls.

sections.heading: Repeat many times, on small batches
sections.intent: Explain mini-batch training and why the loss usually falls in a bumpy way rather than straight down.

lessons.task: Write down the training loop in four steps in your own words, using the words 'forward', 'loss', 'backward', 'update'. Then explain what would happen if the learning rate were a hundred times too large.
quiz: What are the four steps of every training loop?
What does the backward pass calculate?
What is the likely symptom of a learning rate that is far too large?

lessons.title: Training, validating and spotting overfitting
lessons.goal: Train a network while watching the training and validation curves, and recognise overfitting when you see it.

sections.heading: Three sets of data, three jobs
sections.intent: Explain the roles of training, validation and test data for a neural network, and why the validation set is not optional.

sections.heading: Reading a learning curve
sections.intent: Describe a healthy curve (both losses falling) and a broken one (training loss falling while validation loss rises).

sections.heading: What is overfitting
sections.intent: Explain overfitting as memorising the training examples, with the handwriting digit example.

sections.heading: The four usual cures
sections.intent: Introduce more data, data augmentation, dropout and early stopping, in plain words, and say which is the first to try.

lessons.task: Draw a sketch of a healthy learning curve and a sketch of an overfitting one, label both axes, and write one sentence naming the first thing you would try when you see the second one.
quiz: Which set of data is used to decide when to stop training?
What does a validation loss that rises while the training loss falls tell you?
Name two ways to reduce overfitting.

lessons.title: Your first network in Keras
lessons.goal: Build, compile, train and evaluate a classifier for handwritten digits with a few lines of Keras.

sections.heading: The shape of the code
sections.intent: Walk through the four Keras steps: build, compile, train, evaluate, with the shape of the data stated at each step.

sections.heading: The compile step is where you choose the loss
sections.intent: Explain loss, optimizer and metrics in the terms of the previous lessons.

sections.heading: Pixels are numbers between 0 and 1
sections.intent: Explain the standard preparation step of scaling pixel values and reshaping a flat list of pixels into a grid.

sections.heading: Read the evaluation output
sections.intent: Explain the test accuracy and test loss, and what a result of 98 percent means for a ten class problem.

lessons.task: Build a small Keras model for the bundled digits data: an input layer of 64 pixels, one hidden layer of 32 ReLU units and an output layer of 10 classes. Train it for five epochs and record the test accuracy.
quiz: What are the four stages of a Keras training script?
Where do you choose the loss function?
Why are pixel values usually scaled to the range 0 to 1?

project.brief: Classify handwritten digits. Build a neural network on the bundled digits dataset, train it with a validation split, watch the learning curves, and report the test accuracy with an honest description of what the model does and where it fails.
deliverables: A public GitHub repository with a README that states the architecture, the training settings and the result.
A training script that reproduces the reported accuracy with one command.
A predictions file for the test rows that the report recomputes the accuracy from.
A test file that passes in CI on every push.
A short section in the README naming two digits the model confuses and why you think that happens.

rubric.criterion: The network is built and trained reproducibly with a stated configuration
The reported accuracy is computed from the predictions and beats the majority baseline
Overfitting is checked and the failure cases are described honestly

kit.dataset: The bundled scikit-learn digits dataset: 1797 images of 8 by 8 greyscale digits with 10 classes, loaded with sklearn.datasets.load_digits. The kit fixes the split: rows 0 to 1199 are the training rows and rows 1200 to 1796 are the evaluation rows.
artifacts: src/digit_model.py - the learner implements train_and_predict() and build_report().
artifacts/predictions.csv - one row per evaluation digit with index, true label and predicted label; the report recomputes the accuracy and the confusion matrix from this file.
artifacts/training_config.json - the configuration the learner used, with keys hidden_layers, activation_function, epochs and used_validation_split.
